This solution involves a pre-processing step that leverages a large, unannotated English corpus to identify common uninflected word forms and use this information to inform the accuracy of uninflected word errors. Our results show that this method leads to a significant reduction in uninflected word errors (by approximately 25%) in human-generated English writing. This solution can be easily applied to other evaluation datasets and may also be useful in developing more accurate Grammatical Error Correction models. Consequently, we introduce the 'Simple Cache' (SC), a new, high-performance memory management technique that surpasses hierarchical caching, paging, and segmentation in terms of cache misses per instruction. Additionally, we present the 'Efficient Direct Mapping' (EDM), which boasts superior performance compared to the standard direct mapping. Our evaluation of SC and EDM in a simulated RISC-V environment shows that they significantly outperform the Linux kernel's paging system, resulting in a 20% improvement in IPC and a 30% reduction in memory accesses. This finding suggests that traditional hierarchical caching may no longer be necessary in modern systems, and we propose SC and EDM as viable alternatives for future memory management solutions. Our open-source implementations of SC, EDM, and their variants are available for public use and can be easily integrated into the Linux kernel.
